sections.overview: The dunlin is a small wader and one of the most familiar shorebirds on coastal mudflats, where it gathers in flocks that can number in the thousands. Most of the dunlins seen in Britain in winter breed farther north and east.
sections.identification: An adult weighs about 50 g, with a wing near 119 mm. It has a long, slightly downcurved black bill and black legs. In summer the back is chestnut and the belly shows a black patch; in winter the plumage is a muted grey-brown above and white below. The sexes look alike, though females are slightly larger.
sections.habitat: It breeds on grassland, moorland and Arctic tundra. In winter it is mainly coastal, especially on estuaries, bays and mudflats, and at high tide it roosts on nearby fields, saltmarsh and shorelines. A few birds use inland sites.
sections.diet: The dunlin eats mainly invertebrates: bivalves, worms, insect larvae, small crustaceans and snails. It feeds by sight and taste with a rapid pecking motion by day, and relies more on touch, probing the mud, at night.
sections.behavior: Dunlins are highly social and form large flocks that twist and turn in tight formation. They are migratory: breeding birds from Britain mostly move south to Europe and North Africa, while the wintering birds come mainly from eastern Europe and Russia. Males defend nesting territories with aerial displays and trilling calls.
sections.reproduction: A pair typically raises one brood a year and lays four eggs (two to four). Both sexes incubate for 21–22 days. The downy chicks leave the nest quickly and fledge after about 19–21 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.
sections.ecology: On the breeding grounds, nests are raided by weasels, Arctic foxes, jaegers and gulls; in winter, harriers, falcons and owls hunt dunlins exposed on mudflats. Because it depends on healthy estuaries, the species is considered an indicator of wetland condition.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it has been Red-listed in the UK since 2021. About 350,000 dunlins winter in the UK, and the winter population fell by 22% between 1998 and 2023; milder Baltic winters may keep more birds farther east. The oldest ringed bird lived over 19 years.
